card vi-sysdiag-proto  [proto]
Prototype: fold werk's own decided set into one dependency diagram, then change one card
why: Three decided cards rest on an untested assumption — that an agent can read a set of decision cards and name the components of the product. #vi-sysdiag-derive, #vi-sysdiag-grain and #vi-sysdiag-declare are all wrong if it cannot.
subtree: 39 cards, 8 open, 5 proto, 26 decided, 3 unchallenged

Scope, in order. Nothing outside this list.

1. Fold the decided cards of the werk subtree into one Mermaid file, by hand, per #vi-sysdiag-format. Level 1 and level 2 only, per #vi-sysdiag-zoom.
2. Load Mermaid from a CDN and draw it in a tab beside the tree and the 3D graph.
3. Change one card. Redraw with the old file in context. Record whether the result is local or a restructure, per #vi-sysdiag-declare.

Not in scope: the data flow diagram, because #vi-flow says werk is the one project where it cannot be trusted. Not in scope: any layout code, per #vi-sysdiag-format:opt0. Not in scope: automating the fold — step 1 is done by hand, to find out what the fold needs before a command wraps it.

What it can show is false:

- the card set does not name components, only views and schema and build steps
- the same card set folds two different ways on two reads, so there is no stable diagram to be continuous with
- every one-card change reads as a restructure, which would mean the drawing carries no reusable structure

First, a trap to avoid. A depends_on edge between two cards is not an arrow between two parts.

#werk-shots depends_on #werk-pane. That means the screenshot decision needed the pane decision first. It does not mean the screenshot code calls the pane. Same word, two graphs, two meanings.

Second, what the empty arrows mean. We decided what the parts are. We never decided how they talk. The diagram makes that visible for the first time. An empty arrow is a question to answer, not data to fetch — see #vi-sysdiag-ask.

So the arrows come from the cards, once the cards exist. Reading them out of the prototype code would hide the gap instead of showing it.

=================== vi-sysdiag-grid
card vi-sysdiag-grid  [proto]
Grid resolver: the agent draws the diagram on a topological grid, a tile grammar checks it, a program renders it
why: #vi-sysdiag-intent only lets the agent control which cards sit in which row. Edges, labels and spacing are left to the resolver, and six rounds of fixes on #vi-sysdiag-render-polish show the agent cannot see what it produced without rendering and screenshotting. A grid the agent writes cell by cell is legible to its own author before anything is rendered.
subtree: 20 cards, 2 open, 2 proto, 16 decided

Eryks design, three parts: reuse Mermaid syntax for relations, card content and ids; add a grid DSL for placement, constrained by formal adjacency rules; render the checked grid with a deterministic program and parametrised components.

This is the same Substance/Style split as #penrose - Mermaid says what exists, the grid says where it goes - applied to a medium the author can read back.

**The reason this is worth building, stated plainly.** Not control. Legibility. Every defect this session was found by Eryk looking at a picture, never by me reading the input. An intent file cannot be proofread. A grid can: it is a low-fidelity rendering of itself. That closes the loop #vi-sysdiag-lint only half closed - the checker catches what it has a rule for, the grid shows everything else.

**Prior art, none of it invented here.** #tiling-systems is the formal name for rules 1.1 to 1.7. #wang-wfc is the same constraint structure solved generatively. #kandinsky is exactly boxes-on-coarse-grid, edges-on-fine-grid, and warns that optimising it is NP-complete. #svgbob is a working text-grid-to-SVG renderer. #css-grid-areas is the DSL, already shipped, with the rectangle rule and the same-token-count rule worth copying verbatim.

**Three decisions that have to be made before any code.** See the notes on this card.

  -> refines         vi-sysdiag-render  The agent places. A program does the pixel arithmetic and checks it
  -> supported_by    tiling-systems  Tiling systems / recognizable picture languages: the formal name for a 2D language defined by allowed tiles
  -> supported_by    wang-wfc  Wang tiles and Wave Function Collapse: the same constraints, run generatively instead of as a check
  -> supported_by    kandinsky  The Kandinsky model: boxes on a coarse grid, edges routed on a finer grid
  -> supported_by    svgbob  svgbob, ditaa, a2s: working implementations of text grid in, styled SVG out
  -> supported_by    css-grid-areas  CSS grid-template-areas: the mainstream DSL that is already ASCII-art placement with a validity rule
  -> supported_by    penrose  Penrose: Substance says what exists, Style says how it looks, and Substance holds no numbers
  -> alternative_to  vi-sysdiag-intent  The intent file: nested groups, rows, and edges with a colour class. Eight keywords
  <- refines         vi-sysdiag-grid-mvp  What the author writes: the grid's tokens  (14 cards, 1 proto, 13 decided)

  <- depends_on      vi-sysdiag-grid-uturn  A U-turn in an edge is a build warning, not an error
  <- depends_on      vi-sysdiag-link  The card ids on the diagram are a live two-way link, not a footnote
  <- depends_on      vi-sysdiag-grid-offcentre  A single edge that leaves a card off its middle is a build warning

One diagram file. Redraw it whole each turn, with the old drawing in context
why: The scope of a redraw is a judgement, not a lookup. Given the changed card and the whole current diagram, the agent can see whether this is a renamed box or a wrong grouping, and choose a minimal edit or a rethink. A fine-grained dirty mark hands it the answer to that question before it asks it.
